chapter: Army service and after the war
title: The band's music book stolen after he went in
summary: Pianist George Salsbury finished the night; McShann told John Tomino to take the music home but it was stolen from the stand, so the band could not carry on.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I said, 'well, wait a minute, I'll find somebody to play in my place.' I found Salsbury, so he told me he'd finish the night on piano.
Who?

George Salsbury, the piano player there in Kansas City. And so I called John to me and I said, these guys are taking me to Leavenworth. I says, talk to them. So John Termin talked to them. He couldn't make no headway. So John said, well, yeah, you're going to have to go.

I says, well, okay. I said, well, John, I tell you what you do. Now, look, of all the things that you do tonight, get that music and take it home with you tonight and keep it. He said, well, what about the band, don't you want the band to -- he says, 'we've got all these dates, ain't no need of missing this money. I can be sending you this money while you're in the service.'

He says, 'we're booked a year ahead.' I said, 'well, in that case, here's what we'll do. Go ahead on and if everybody in the band agrees, they want to go ahead on and finish these dates, finish the dates.' I said, 'but take that music home with you tonight.' I says, 'and I will ask you to take it -- I had about four or five changes of uniforms then, and I said, 'I will ask you to take the uniforms, too, but I know it's going to be hard to get somebody up here. But if you can get somebody, get them up here and get these trunks and have the uniforms put in the trunks.'

I said, 'but if you don't do nothing but take the music home --' he says, 'okay, okay,' but he didn't. He didn't take the music home and he came down the next day. The fellow says, well, I don't know, there was two fellows came in here, and they got a thing off the bandstand and that's the only thing they got.
Oh, no!
Which was the music.
How did they know? Who was it?
Never did find out.
That's very strange, because there's not much point in taking the music if you're not going to do something with it.

That's true. The only thing we ever heard was that a number that we had in the book (unintelligible). And I heard an arrangement of that. But it wasn't the same arrangement, by Hamp. But I never did hear none of the rest of the stuff.
Well, Jay, so you mean to say that the music is gone, then they had no band?
I lost the whole book. And then so the band couldn't go.
John must have wanted to cut his throat.
If he'd have known who had taken it, I'm sure, but they didn't have no way of knowing who took the book.
Yeah, but you told him to take it.

I told John, I says, of all the things you do, take care of that book, get that music. Because I know, by me not being there, you know what I mean, I figured -- I just had that feeling. And we never did find that book.
That's terrible.
Well, did the band carry on after this?
They tried to, but some of the guys left town and some didn't. They got to Cincinnati and a couple of three places, wasn't -- they didn't have the book, so they was messed up, anyway.
What happened to the uniforms?

Those uniforms just got -- same difference, you know what I mean. But they didn't take the uniforms when they took the book. See, after -- well, the guys -- some of the uniforms was missing and some wasn't. Some was missing and some of them wasn't.
